text: An operating system update for the DB instance (`system-update` on an instance ARN). It does not change the DB engine version or the DB instance class.

This cannot be expressed in code. The Terraform `aws_db_instance`, CloudFormation `AWS::RDS::DBInstance` and CDK resources have a maintenance window, auto minor version upgrade and an engine version, and no argument that applies a pending maintenance action. No code change is needed and none causes drift: the operating system level is not an attribute of the resource.

AWS publishes no CVE list for this action: it returns the action, its dates and a generic description. AWS says operating system updates most often occur for security issues and recommends applying them as soon as possible.

Operating system updates typically take about 10 minutes. On a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment RDS patches the standby, promotes it, then patches the old primary: one failover that typically lasts less than a minute. A Single-AZ instance is offline while it is patched.

An optional update has no apply date and RDS never applies it automatically. A mandatory update has an apply date: after it RDS applies the update in a maintenance window, and moving the window does not avoid it (after the mandatory date RDS can apply it outside the preferred window).

The person running this needs `rds:DescribePendingMaintenanceActions`, `rds:ApplyPendingMaintenanceAction`, `rds:DescribeDBInstances`, `rds:DescribeEvents` and `rds:CreateDBSnapshot` on this instance, and AWS CLI access to the account and Region.
Confirm the action is still pending and read its dates (a mandatory update has `AutoAppliedAfterDate` and `CurrentApplyDate`; an optional one has neither).
The instance must be `available`. Read whether it is Multi-AZ and when its maintenance window is. Changes waiting for the window are in `PendingModifiedValues`, not in the pending maintenance list.
An `immediate` opt-in can't be undone. Take a manual snapshot first so there is a known restore point.
RDS console, Region {region} > Databases > select `{id}` > Actions > Patch at next window (or Patch now). Defer upgrade stays available until the update starts.
Schedule it for the next maintenance window.
Or apply it now, in a quiet period. An immediate opt-in can't be undone.

The action leaves the pending list once applied. The list is eventually consistent: right after applying it can still show the action. Poll with backoff, starting at a couple of seconds, for up to five minutes, then check the instance is `available` again.

A scheduled update that has not started can be cancelled with `undo-opt-in`. Once it has started it can't be deferred, and an immediate opt-in can't be undone. AWS documents no way to remove an applied operating system update; the restore point is the snapshot.

An engine version upgrade (`db-upgrade`). It is the one pending maintenance action with a code equivalent: raising the engine version in code does the same thing and keeps the code and the database aligned.
This has a code equivalent: the engine version attribute of the database resource. Applying it in AWS instead leaves a version pinned in code behind the live one.
The pending action carries no CVE list. A CVE is named here only when an AWS bulletin ties it to this engine and target version.

Change `engine_version` on the `aws_db_instance` (or the module input or variable that feeds it). It is an in-place update. A major version jump also needs `allow_major_version_upgrade = true` and a parameter group of the new family in `parameter_group_name`.

`apply_immediately` defaults to `false`: after apply the upgrade is queued for the next maintenance window, and the plan keeps showing a difference until it runs. With `apply_immediately = true` the outage happens at apply time, which in an apply-on-merge pipeline is at merge.

`engine_version` updates in place. The provider documents `backup_target`, `nchar_character_set_name`, `restore_to_point_in_time` and `multi_tenant` (true to false) as forcing a new resource. CoderHelm also refuses a change to `identifier`, `identifier_prefix` or `snapshot_identifier` in an upgrade change, to stay on the safe side: check the plan for "must be replaced".

If the live version is already ahead of the pinned `engine_version` (auto minor version upgrade defaults to `true`), the next apply asks RDS for a lower version and RDS refuses it (`InvalidParameterCombination`: cannot upgrade from the higher version to the lower one), which blocks every apply of that root. Never set a value below the live version. The provider fix for `aws_db_instance` was still an open pull request on the review date.

With auto minor version upgrade enabled the provider accepts a version prefix (`8.0` for `8.0.36`) and reports the running version as `engine_version_actual`. A prefix that already covers the target needs no code change; keep the prefix rather than replacing it with a full version.

`blue_green_update { enabled = true }` performs the update through an RDS Blue/Green deployment (MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL only, not with replicas, backups must be enabled). Switchover downtime is usually under one minute. Do not add it as part of this change unless the team asks: it changes how every later update of the instance is applied.

Change `EngineVersion` on the `AWS::RDS::DBInstance` (or the parameter that feeds it). Update requires: Some interruptions (in place, not a replacement). A major version jump also needs `AllowMajorVersionUpgrade: true`.

CloudFormation applies DB instance updates immediately by default (`ApplyImmediately` defaults to `true`): the outage happens when the stack update runs. With `ApplyImmediately: false` the change waits for the next maintenance window and the instance stays in a drift state until then.

`EngineVersion` is not a replacement property. `DBInstanceIdentifier`, `DBClusterIdentifier` and `DBSnapshotIdentifier` are: CloudFormation creates a replacement instance, then deletes the old one and its automated snapshots. Changing the logical id of the resource replaces it too.

CloudFormation compares the new template with the previous template, not with the live database. If AWS already moved the version forward, the stale template value is invisible until someone edits it. Set the value to at least the live version. A version prefix (`16`, `8.0`) is matched by prefix during drift detection.
RDS Blue/Green Deployments are not supported with CloudFormation. Do not propose one for a stack-managed database.

Change the engine version on the instance's `engine` (for example `rds.PostgresEngineVersion.VER_17_7` or `rds.MysqlEngineVersion.VER_8_0_39`; use the class's static `of(...)` when the library has no constant for the target). CDK passes it to `EngineVersion`, an in-place update. A major version jump also needs `allowMajorVersionUpgrade: true` (default false).
The change applies when the stack deploys. To schedule instance modifications for the next maintenance window set `applyImmediately: false` on the instance.

Changing a construct id changes the logical id, and CloudFormation then replaces the resource. Keep every construct id and the instance identifier as they are. The default `removalPolicy` is SNAPSHOT.

Engine upgrades require downtime. Multi-AZ does not avoid it for a DB instance deployment: primary and standby are upgraded at the same time and both are unavailable, and a minor upgrade can last several minutes. A Multi-AZ DB cluster typically limits a minor upgrade to about 35 seconds (one second or less behind RDS Proxy). A Single-AZ instance is offline for the length of the upgrade; AWS gives no figure. RDS for MySQL major upgrades typically complete in about 10 minutes.

The person running this needs `rds:DescribeDBEngineVersions`, `rds:DescribeDBInstances`, `rds:CreateDBSnapshot`, `rds:ModifyDBInstance` (or `rds:ApplyPendingMaintenanceAction`) and `rds:DescribeEvents` on this instance.
Confirm the target is a valid upgrade from the running version (the row with `AutoUpgrade` true is the version RDS moves to on its own).

Read replicas change the order. RDS for MySQL: upgrade every read replica before the source instance. RDS for PostgreSQL major upgrade: in-Region replicas are upgraded together with the primary and can lengthen its downtime. Multi-AZ DB cluster read replicas: for a minor upgrade, upgrade the replicas first or the upgrade is blocked.

For a major upgrade: have a parameter group of the new family ready; apply pending operating system updates first; PostgreSQL needs no open prepared transactions, no logical replication slots on source versions before 17, and extensions that the target supports; MySQL goes one major version at a time (5.7 to 8.0, then 8.0 to 8.4) and runs mandatory prechecks that cancel the upgrade before the instance stops (details in `PrePatchCompatibility.log`).
Test the upgrade on a copy first: restore a snapshot into a new instance, upgrade that instance and run the application's tests against it.
Take a manual snapshot before the upgrade. RDS takes its own snapshots before and after an upgrade only when the backup retention period is greater than 0.

RDS console, Region {region} > Databases > select `{id}` > Modify > DB engine version: {target} > Continue > choose Apply during the next scheduled maintenance window (or Apply immediately) > Modify DB instance.
Upgrade in the next maintenance window. Add `--allow-major-version-upgrade` for a major version jump; use `--apply-immediately` to upgrade now.

During the upgrade the status is `upgrading` and the instance can't be modified. Afterwards the status is `available` and the engine version is the target. After a PostgreSQL major upgrade run `ANALYZE VERBOSE;` in every database and update extensions with `ALTER EXTENSION name UPDATE`.

Upgrades are one-way: after the upgrade you can't revert to the previous engine version. The way back is restoring the pre-upgrade snapshot into a new DB instance, which loses every write since the snapshot. Reverting the version in code is not a rollback: it asks RDS for a downgrade, which RDS refuses. RDS rolls back by itself only when the upgrade fails.

With auto minor version upgrade on, RDS upgrades in the maintenance window to the version it has flagged for automatic upgrade. With it off, RDS still upgrades for critical security issues or when the version reaches its end of support, and after a mandatory date it can do so outside the preferred window.
